title: 'The land is ours': First Nation intends to mine sand in Manitoba through Sio Silica partnership
summary: A Manitoba First Nation is planning to push ahead with a proposed sand mining operation to support a solar panel manufacturing facility, whether the provincial government likes it or not.

image.caption: Sheldon Kent, chief of Black River First Nation, would like the province to grant a licence for Sio Silica to harvest high purity quartz sand on First Nation land, but said the project will go ahead regardless. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba
A Manitoba First Nation is planning to push ahead with a proposed sand mining operation to support a solar panel manufacturing facility, whether the provincial government likes it or not.
'We have our own right to do it and we're going do this project,' says Black River Chief Sheldon Kent
Sheldon Kent, chief of Black River First Nation on the east shore of Lake Winnipeg, said his community is partnering with mining company Sio Silica to harvest high-purity quartz.
"We see the environmental plan [for the Sio Silica project] is sustainable, it's workable, it's safe," he said Monday at a news conference with the Southern Chiefs' Organization.
"We wouldn't get involved if it was going to be destructive and destroy what we have."
Kent said he's asking the province to work with Black River, but "we have our own jurisdiction, we have our own right to do it, and we're going to do this project" on First Nation land.

Specifically, he's talking about just over 1,000 hectares (2,500 acres) of land near near Vivian, about 50 kilometres east of Winnipeg. His community bought the land a few years ago because it saw economic potential, he said.
Kent expects sand harvesting to start as early as next year.

items: Sio Silica promises $125M sand-storage facility in Churchill, Man., if mining licence approved

blocks.text: The ideal scenario would be that Manitoba's NDP government grants a licence, Kent said, "but from a First Nations stand, the land is ours. We've always maintained and protected the land, [and] we are going to go forward with or without the province.
"I don't need to go to court. I'm just going to go occupy the land that we already have and we'll start mining it."
CBC News has reached out to the province for a response.
Southern Chiefs’ Organization Grand Chief Jerry Daniels is working toward acquiring up to 51 per cent ownership in a facility that would manufacture solar panels in Manitoba. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)
Kent spoke after Southern Chiefs' Grand Chief Jerry Daniels announced a preliminary agreement with German manufacturer RCT Solutions in a solar project that will rely on the sand.
The organization is working toward acquiring up to 51 per cent ownership in a facility that would manufacture solar panels and glass "here in Manitoba," said Daniels.
"An ownership stake could give our nations a say in how the facility is developed [and] operated, and share in the returns it will generate."
Those returns, particularly financial resources, could then be invested and used to support First Nations communities and their quality of life, he said.

"Opportunities like this can help a young person in one of our nations to learn a trade, build a career and raise a family close to home," said Daniels, adding First Nations businesses would also be able to bid on work to build, supply and operate the facility.

Peter Fath, CEO of the German manufacturer RCT Solutions, wants to build a solar panel production campus but says the company needs the high-quality sand that Sio Silica would mine. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)

The head and founder of RCT Solutions, Peter Fath, said in July 2023 that he wanted to build a multibillion-dollar solar panel production campus near Winnipeg, which he said would employ close to 8,000 people.
"My solar sector is growing like hell, but we don't have enough high-purity quartz. You have the fuel of our industry," Fath said at Monday's news conference.
All four stages needed in the production chain of solar panels "are perfectly tagged by the quartz quality of Sio Silica," he added.
Sio Silica is hoping to obtain an environmental licence to drill for sand in the rural municipality of Springfield, but Premier Wab Kinew cast doubt in June on the prospect of Manitoba approving it.

items: Kinew casts doubt on approving Sio Silica's 2nd effort to obtain licence to mine sand

blocks.text: Kinew's NDP government denied an earlier Sio Silica application in 2024.
Fath said Manitoba, with its hydro and power, has a chance to become a green manufacturing hub of Canada with the addition of his company's solar panel manufacturing campus.
He was more conciliatory in his messaging to the province, saying without its support, "it will not work."
"I will not run against the wall and get a bloody head," Fath said.
The sand below the surface of southeastern Manitoba is 99.85 per cent pure silica. (Gary Solilak/CBC)
As for where the solar campus idea currently stands, he said it needs an engineering study and a feasibility study on a possible location. After that, an investment decision needs to be made.
Three potential sites have been identified but no location has been chosen, he said.
Fath said he's puzzled by the pushback to the Sio Silica project.

Everyone needs energy and wants it to be green, and Manitoba is sitting on "white gold," he said. The province has one of the world's largest deposits of quartz-rich silica, which could enable it to "build its own future," said Fath.
He repeated past claims it will be mined in a safe, sustainable way, and disputed concerns the process could contaminate drinking water.
"Let us work on fact-driven decisions," he said. "If I had any doubt on the negative environmental impact … I would not do the project, definitely not."
If anything did force a halt to mining, "I would lose hundreds of millions of dollars [of dollars] with my partners," said Fath.
